Using Claude to Organize Project Requirements

Turn scattered notes into a requirement register while keeping assumptions, contradictions and decisions visible.

By DevMania · 21 September 2026 · 2 min read

In this guide

Start with a bounded collection of notesAsk for traceable entriesUse an ERP exampleDefine the output before running the taskMove approved decisions into your project record

Start with a bounded collection of notes

Project information often arrives through messages, meeting notes and spreadsheets. Claude can help organize supplied text, but the first task should be classification rather than invention. Explain the project purpose and ask for requirements, open questions and contradictions as separate outputs. This creates a reviewable structure without pretending the notes are complete.

Ask for traceable entries

Give each source note a label and request that every requirement references the note supporting it. For example, a customer portal requirement could cite “Workshop A, item 6.” The labels are your own working references, not evidence that the assistant independently verified the statement. Check each important entry against its source before approval.

Use an ERP example

Suppose one note says every employee can add suppliers and another says only purchasing staff can do so. Ask Claude to surface the conflict instead of choosing one silently. Record an owner for the decision. This prevents an uncertain permission rule from becoming application behaviour just because it appeared in a polished requirements table.

Define the output before running the task

Request columns for requirement, user role, source, priority and unresolved question. Claude’s prompting guidance emphasizes clear task instructions; in this workflow, the table also makes review easier. Keep priority provisional until the business owner confirms it. The assistant cannot know your budget or contractual commitments from a vague note.

Move approved decisions into your project record

After reviewing the output, keep a versioned requirement register and a short change log. Mark which decisions are confirmed and which remain open. Use the organized notes as input to design and estimation, then revisit them when the process changes. The value lies in reducing ambiguity, not merely producing a longer document.
